headline: GTA VI pre-orders confirmed for June 25, sending Take-Two surging nearly 6% last night — the biggest mover in your portfolio this session.

movers.name: Take-Two Interactive
movers.note: Rockstar Games confirmed GTA VI pre-orders open June 25, and the market went bananas — this is the moment investors have been waiting years for. The stock jumped ~6% last night, pushing your holding into profit (+$29.82 AUD overall). Barron's called the boost 'years in the making' and analysts expect pre-order numbers to be massive.

movers.name: Pilbara Minerals
movers.note: Pilbara slid nearly 3% today, continuing the rough patch for ASX lithium stocks. The spodumene (raw lithium mineral) price is still under pressure, and while there's some chatter about a potential price recovery signal, there's no concrete catalyst yet. You're down about 8.5% on this one overall.

movers.name: Alphabet Inc. (Google)
movers.note: Google had a strong night last session, up 1.2%. Recent earnings showed Alphabet beat expectations by a wide margin and doubled its cloud backlog to $460 billion — that's a huge pipeline of future revenue. The AI and advertising business is firing, and analysts remain constructive on the stock.

movers.name: Global X Artificial Intelligence ETF
movers.note: GXAI nudged up 1% today, riding positive sentiment from AI stocks broadly. The ETF tracks global AI companies, so Google's strong results and the broader tech rally last night in the US filtered through. Still down about 4% overall from your entry.

movers.name: Vanguard FTSE Emerging Markets ETF
movers.note: Emerging markets had a decent session today, up 0.82%. A slightly weaker Aussie dollar (which makes overseas assets worth more in AUD terms when converted back) gave this ETF a small tailwind. You're barely in the green overall — just 59 cents profit.

movers.name: Vanguard Diversified High Growth ETF
movers.note: VDHG dipped slightly today, down 0.37%. As a diversified fund with heavy US exposure, it tends to follow global market sentiment. Nothing alarming — just a mild pullback after a solid recent run. You're up $3.75 overall.

movers.name: Vanguard US Total Market Shares ETF
movers.note: VTS edged down 0.32% today. This ETF tracks the entire US sharemarket, and the slight dip likely reflects the ASX pricing in some overnight caution before the US session. Last night the US markets were actually up strongly, so expect this to look better tomorrow. You're up $4.09 overall.

movers.name: Microsoft
movers.note: Microsoft was basically flat last night, down just 4 cents. There's no major news catalyst — it's holding ground while the market focuses on Google's AI story. You're still down about $57.92 AUD on this position overall, so it remains the main drag in your portfolio.

movers.name: BetaShares Global Energy Companies ETF
movers.note: FUEL slipped 0.85% today, which makes sense — oil (WTI crude) dropped 2.5% last night to $74.91 a barrel. The IEA flagged that the Iran-related supply shock is fading as Strait of Hormuz flows resume, and the IMF says prices should ease rather than crash. Lower oil price = lower energy company revenues = this ETF dips.

watch_today.title: TTWO: GTA VI pre-orders open June 25 — momentum building
watch_today.detail: Rockstar officially confirmed GTA VI pre-orders start next Wednesday. Last night's 5.84% jump is just the beginning — the actual pre-order numbers will be the next big catalyst. This has been years in the making and your position is now +$29.82 AUD. Consider whether you want to hold through the pre-order hype or trim some profit.

watch_today.title: PLS.AX: Lithium still under pressure — watch for more downside
watch_today.detail: Pilbara fell another 3% today and is now down 8.5% on your entry. Spodumene prices (the raw material Pilbara sells) remain weak, and there's no clear price recovery yet despite some analyst optimism. The IEA's demand forecasts aren't helping either. Keep a close eye this week — if it breaks below $6.00 that's a meaningful support level gone.

watch_today.title: GOOG: Earnings beat + $460B cloud backlog = still a strong story
watch_today.detail: Alphabet recently beat earnings by 94% (per 24/7 Wall St.) and doubled its cloud revenue backlog to $460 billion. Last night's 1.2% gain adds to that momentum. The AI tailwind — from both Google Search AI and Google Cloud — looks durable. Your position is up 19.2% overall.

watch_today.title: Oil drop hurts FUEL.AX — Hormuz reopening changes the energy picture
watch_today.detail: Crude oil fell 2.5% last night to $74.91 as the Strait of Hormuz (a critical shipping channel for Middle East oil) resumes normal flows after the Iran conflict. The IEA now flags a potential oil glut (too much supply). If that trend continues, FUEL.AX faces further headwinds this week.

watch_today.title: RBA rate path: Some economists say more hikes are coming
watch_today.detail: Despite the RBA's recent pause, a number of economists (per AFR today) are warning more rate rises could still be on the table. Higher rates for longer are generally bad for growth stocks and property — worth keeping in mind for your VDHG and VTS holdings, which have significant Australian and US equity exposure.

watch_today.title: CGT reform update: Chalmers scales back ministerial powers to get Senate support
watch_today.detail: Treasurer Jim Chalmers is winding back the government's proposed capital gains tax (CGT) changes — specifically trimming ministerial discretion powers — to try to get the Senate to pass the reforms. This matters if you ever sell holdings at a profit: CGT is the tax you pay on investment gains. The rules are still in flux, so worth watching how this plays out in the Senate.

markets.summary: Last night's US session was a solid green day — the S&P 500 climbed 1.05% to 7,497 and the NASDAQ jumped 1.61% to 26,441, driven by tech strength. Google was a standout gainer. However, gold fell sharply (down 2.56% to $4,247/oz) and oil dropped 2.45% to $74.91 — both suggesting some of the 'fear premium' that had been built into commodity prices is unwinding as Middle East tensions ease. The Aussie dollar slipped to 70.2 US cents. The ASX 200 data wasn't available at close today.

politics.summary: All eyes in Canberra today are on the Labor government's CGT (capital gains tax) reform saga — Chalmers is trying to water down parts of the proposal to get Senate votes, while critics on both sides say it doesn't go far enough or goes too far. Meanwhile, the RBA rate debate is heating up, with some economists warning the cash rate pause might not last.

stories.title: Chalmers scales back CGT changes in bid to pass Senate
stories.why_it_matters: Treasurer Jim Chalmers is trying to remove certain ministerial discretion powers from the CGT reform bill to win over crossbench Senate votes. The original proposal would have raised the CGT discount (the tax break you get when selling investments held over 12 months) and tightened negative gearing on existing properties. The backdown hasn't satisfied critics — the AFR says Labor is still copping flak from both business groups and progressive voices. For investors, the final shape of these rules directly affects how much tax you'd pay when selling shares or property at a profit.

stories.title: Some economists warn more RBA rate hikes are still coming
stories.why_it_matters: While the RBA recently paused its rate-hiking cycle, several economists interviewed by the AFR believe the central bank isn't done yet and may lift rates further. Their argument: inflation isn't fully under control and the labour market is still too tight. Higher rates mean more expensive mortgages, which hurts consumer spending and can weigh on ASX-listed companies that rely on domestic demand.

stories.title: Guardian: RBA's unemployment view slammed as favouring companies over workers
stories.why_it_matters: The Guardian argues the RBA's implicit view that unemployment needs to rise to bring inflation down is a policy choice that protects company profit margins at workers' expense. This is a broader political debate about who bears the cost of taming inflation — and it's relevant because it shapes political pressure on the RBA ahead of any future rate decisions.

stories.title: Albanese government gives ground on tax — but NDIS fight still looms
stories.why_it_matters: The Conversation's Grattan analysis notes Labor has already made concessions on tax policy but faces a harder battle over NDIS (National Disability Insurance Scheme) funding reforms. The government needs Senate support for both packages, and concessions on one could make the other harder to pass. For everyday Australians, NDIS changes affect services for people with disability and the broader federal budget bottom line.

ai.summary: The big AI story today is geopolitical — the CEOs of Anthropic and Google DeepMind used the G7 summit to push for a US-led AI coalition among allied nations. Meanwhile, a conflict-of-interest question is swirling around an AI copyright charity with links to Anthropic donors, and there's a wild AI subscription deal doing the rounds online.

stories.title: OpenAI, Google and Anthropic CEOs join world leaders at G7 — push for US-led AI alliance
stories.why_it_matters: The CEOs of Anthropic and Google DeepMind appeared alongside Trump and other world leaders at the G7, calling for democratic nations to form a coordinated AI coalition — essentially a joint strategy to make sure Western countries, not China, set the global rules for AI. CNBC described it as 'a signal of where power sits' that tech executives now have a seat at the table alongside heads of state. For Google shareholders, Sundar Pichai's presence reinforces that Alphabet is central to the global AI policy conversation, not just a bystander.

stories.title: Charity shaping AI copyright rules has ties to Anthropic-linked donors
stories.why_it_matters: The SMH is reporting that a charity helping shape AI copyright policy — deciding rules around whether AI companies can train their models on copyrighted material — is funded by donors with ties to Anthropic, one of the biggest AI companies. This raises obvious conflict-of-interest concerns: the people bankrolling the rule-makers also stand to benefit from the rules. Copyright law for AI training data is one of the biggest legal battles in tech right now, worth billions in potential liability.

stories.title: Australian banks struggling to adopt AI fast enough due to regulation
stories.why_it_matters: Australian banks want to use AI to cut costs and improve services, but are finding compliance requirements (think: data privacy rules, financial services regulations) are slowing them down significantly. The piece highlights that banks face a real balancing act — move too fast and regulators crack down, move too slow and fintechs eat their lunch. Relevant context for anyone holding Australian bank stocks or broad ASX ETFs like VDHG.

stories.title: ChatGPT Plus $240/yr vs. 5-year bundle of ChatGPT, Claude & Gemini for $99.99
stories.why_it_matters: A deal doing the rounds online lets you get 5 years of access to ChatGPT, Claude (Anthropic's AI), and Gemini (Google's AI) bundled together for just $99.99 — compared to $240 a year for ChatGPT Plus alone. Boing Boing did the maths and it works out to roughly $20/year. Practically speaking, if you haven't tried these tools yet, this is a very cheap way to get across all three major AI assistants at once.

sport.summary: NRL Round 16 kicks off tomorrow night — the Titans host Penrith at Cbus Super Stadium on Saturday, which is the local game to watch on the Gold Coast. In judiciary news, Blues players Staggs and Radley have been fined after Origin. Benji Marshall has opened up about his coaching days, and a Brisbane Broncos star is heading to France. AFL has team news worth flagging too.

stories.title: NRL Judiciary: Staggs and Radley fined after Blues' State of Origin loss
stories.why_it_matters: Both NSW Blues players Apisai Staggs and Victor Radley have been hit with fines by the NRL Judiciary following incidents during the Origin match. Neither was suspended, so they'll be available for their clubs in Round 16. The Blues lost the match, and now individual players are copping financial penalties on top of that — a rough week for NSW fans.

stories.title: Braith Anasta questions Laurie Daley's reappointment as NSW coach
stories.why_it_matters: Former NRL player and Fox Sports commentator Braith Anasta has publicly questioned whether Laurie Daley should have been reappointed as NSW Blues head coach after the Origin loss. It adds to the post-series scrutiny on the Blues' coaching setup and selection. No article text available for further detail, but it's generating plenty of debate.

stories.title: Benji Marshall: 'Got $30k for no minutes'
stories.why_it_matters: Benji Marshall has revealed in a candid interview that he was paid $30,000 during his playing career for a season where he didn't get a single minute on the field. It's an insight into the financial side of NRL contracts — clubs sometimes pay players to sit on the bench or in reserve, particularly for salary cap and roster management reasons. Good behind-the-scenes footy yarn.

stories.title: Catalans Dragons land Brisbane Broncos star in major coup
stories.why_it_matters: A Brisbane Broncos player is heading to the French Super League side Catalans Dragons in what's being called a major signing coup for the European club. No specific player name available from the article text, but it's another sign of the growing pull of European rugby league for NRL players seeking new contracts or experiences.

stories.title: AFL: Cats' goal-line calamity gifts bizarre major to Jackson
stories.why_it_matters: Geelong's defence had an absolute nightmare moment, gifting a bizarre goal to West Coast's Jeremy Jackson via a goal-line bungle. No further match details available from the article text, but the clip is doing the rounds as one of those 'can you believe that?' moments that only AFL delivers. Cats fans will want to look away.
